evals.prompt: I run marketing at Fenlock Systems and we're putting on our first developer conference, FenConf, in Lyon on June 18-19. The marketing plan hands me these fixed dates: public announcement April 2, agenda goes live May 6, doors June 18. Tickets are paid and registration opens with the announcement. We have about 1,200 addresses on our list. I've done lifecycle marketing for our product for years, so my instinct is a proper nurture sequence - something like 8-10 touches, branching on opens and clicks so engaged people get different content than quiet ones, plus a re-engagement branch for people who go cold. Can you design the full sequence and cadence?
evals.expected_output: A dated send map built on the fixed dates, rejecting the behavioural drip in favour of the thin dated arc, with one job per send and the list's provenance checked.
expectations: Rejects the 8-10 touch nurture sequence instead of building it, and proposes roughly 2 to 4 reminder sends across the pre-event arc
Rejects open/click branching as structurally wrong for an event (a fixed, dated arc that ends on one day), not merely as a tooling limitation
Every send in the proposed plan fires on a calendar date; none is conditioned on a recipient's open, click, or inactivity
Presents the thin cadence as what event organizers actually send, not as a budget or reduced version of a real sequence
The default plan is the five-send core arc: announcement, registration confirmation, know-before-you-go, day-before nudge, post-event thank-you
No re-engagement or win-back email appears in the plan for this edition's own registrants
Asks where the 1,200 addresses came from, per source, rather than assuming the whole list is mailable
Maps sends onto the fixed dates given (April 2 announcement, May 6 agenda, June 18 doors) without moving any of them
Restates the handed-down dates back to the user rather than re-deriving or adjusting them
If an agenda-release email is included, it is marked optional or first-to-cut, not core
Each email in the send map carries exactly one stated job
The know-before-you-go lands roughly one week before doors and the day-before nudge the evening before

evals.prompt: Our data engineering conference TidePool Conf (Rotterdam, May 21-22) has early-bird pricing ending Sunday at 23:59. We're at about 40% of the 600-seat capacity. I want a last-call push: one email Thursday and another Sunday morning, and in both let's say tickets are almost gone to get people moving. One more thought - weekend emails perform terribly in our stats, so should we just quietly extend the early-bird to Monday and send the deadline email then? Write me the copy.
evals.expected_output: One last-call email scheduled the day before the real cutoff, targeting only the not-yet-registered, with the true dated fact and no invented scarcity; the double send and the deadline move both refused.
expectations: Refuses to claim tickets are almost gone when the stated figure is 40% of capacity
Distinguishes a true, checkable figure (stating the real number if anything) from manufactured scarcity
Produces exactly one last-call email and declines the Thursday-plus-Sunday double send: one cutoff, one email
Refuses to extend or quietly move the early-bird deadline; the cutoff is treated as fixed and owned by pricing, not by email performance
Schedules the last-call for Saturday, the day before the Sunday 23:59 cutoff
Targets only the not-yet-registered, cross-referenced against the registered list so no ticket holder receives it
The copy states what changes and exactly when, letting the date carry the urgency - no 'last chance', 'don't miss out', countdown, or scarcity phrasing
The subject names TidePool Conf and the deadline plainly, roughly in the 40-60 character range
Preview text extends the subject with an additional usable fact rather than repeating it
The body carries one CTA and one link
The sign-off is a named human, not a team or role
Does not propose a 'deadline extended' follow-up email as an alternative tactic

evals.prompt: We're opening registration for CairnStack 2027, our infrastructure conference in Edinburgh, next month. I have two lists to announce it to: 1,900 addresses exported from last year's ticketing platform (everyone who bought a ticket to CairnStack 2026), and 450 people who signed up to our monthly newsletter through the form on our site, which has an opt-in checkbox for event news. Marketing wants me to merge both and send the announcement to all 2,350. There'll be an unsubscribe link obviously. Anything wrong with that plan before I hit send?
evals.expected_output: A clear do-not-send verdict on the merged blast: the ticket-export addresses lack marketing consent, the newsletter opt-ins are mailable, provenance is recorded per address, and sign-off is required before any prior-edition reuse.
expectations: Evaluates the two address sources separately rather than as one merged list
States that buying a ticket to CairnStack 2026 is not consent to be marketed to for 2027; the 1,900 ticket-export addresses are not mailable without a documented opt-in
Treats the 450 newsletter addresses, with their explicit event-news opt-in, as mailable
States what the ticket transaction did consent to: the confirmation, the practical information, and changes to it - not promotional sends
Rejects the unsubscribe link as a substitute for consent
Requires provenance recorded per address - which form, which edition, which box was ticked, and when - not per list
Names the exposure as irreversible: the kind of mistake that can force a list deletion the event never recovers from, not merely poor practice
Requires sign-off or a compliance check before any reuse of the prior-edition list
Gives a clear do-not-send verdict on the merged 2,350-address send as planned
Notes the announcement, being non-transactional, must carry a working unsubscribe honoured immediately
Offers the compliant scope: announce now to the 450 opted-in addresses
Frames the rules as jurisdiction-dependent and to be checked for where attendees are, rather than asserting one blanket regime

evals.prompt: Please write the practical-info email for BarnOwl Conf, 350 attendees, Manchester, October 8-9. Here's everything from the ops team: check-in opens 8:15 both days at Whitworth Hall's main entrance on Oak Street 14, second floor via the east staircase, bring photo ID, badges are printed on site and must be worn; no cloakroom, so no large luggage; lunch and two coffee breaks are provided and dietary choices from registration are catered; wifi available; quiet room on floor 3; step-free access via the north entrance lift, and live captioning on both stages; sponsors are Datashore, Kestrel Cloud and Plinth. One thing: a separate tool called SafeDesk will email everyone about incident reporting a few days before the event - that's out of our hands. Keep the email short and skimmable: skip the code of conduct section (it's on the website and nobody reads it twice), and we have no nursing room so just leave that whole topic out.
evals.expected_output: A complete know-before-you-go that keeps the code of conduct and accessibility sections, states the nursing-room absence, announces the SafeDesk email by name and timing, and marks missing sections as not applicable rather than inventing facts.
expectations: The code of conduct section is kept despite the instruction to cut it, with a link, the stated enforcement consequence, and a contact route
The refusal is explained: code of conduct and accessibility decide whether someone attends at all, so they are never a length trade-off
An accessibility section appears covering the given provisions (step-free north-entrance lift, live captioning), what must be requested and by when, and who to ask
The nursing/parents' room absence is stated explicitly in the email rather than silently omitted
The SafeDesk email is announced in advance inside this email, by name and timing
The reason is present: an unannounced, differently-branded automated email gets reported as phishing or ignored as spam
The email opens with event name, exact dates, and the daily opening time - no teaser or hook opener
Check-in is a walked sequence: main entrance on Oak Street 14, east staircase to the second floor, photo ID ready, badges printed on site and worn
The no-cloakroom / no-large-luggage restriction is included
The venue address appears in plain text, not only inside a map or image
Sections with no supplied facts (transit, parking, airport directions, evening events) are marked not applicable or flagged as facts to obtain - never invented
The email closes with sponsor thanks naming Datashore, Kestrel Cloud and Plinth
A completeness check is run or reported: every section present or explicitly not applicable, with a partial pass treated as a fail

evals.prompt: Our free community event NorthStack Night runs its big annual edition on November 5 - 500 registered, the venue fits 350, and historically about 40% of free registrants don't show. I'm worried about both directions: too many people if everyone comes, too few if the usual crowd flakes. My plan is a reminder email every day of the final week to keep it top of mind, and I'd like to know how many extra registrations we should accept over 350 to compensate for the flaking. We also have the broader NorthStack community list (2,800 people, opted in) - should I keep emailing the ones who haven't registered until they do? What would you actually send?
evals.expected_output: The daily countdown chain refused in favour of the week-before plus day-before pair, non-registered follow-ups capped at two and cross-referenced, and the overbooking arithmetic routed out as a separate structural problem.
expectations: Rejects the reminder-every-day final-week plan (a countdown chain) instead of adopting it
Explains the cost in list terms: each extra send trains recipients to stop opening the one that matters
Recommends the week-before know-before-you-go plus a short day-before nudge as the reminder pair
Cites the 30-50% signup-to-attendance drop-off for free events as what makes the reminders load-bearing
Does not compute or recommend an overbooking or over-registration number
Reminder emails are presented as this plan's lever against no-shows, while overbooking, waitlists, deposits and seat-release are named as structural fixes owned by a separate no-show process
Follow-ups to not-yet-registered community members are capped at one, maximum two
Follow-ups are cross-referenced against the registered list so no registrant is asked to register
Send caps are counted per segment, not across the whole list
The day-before nudge carries only when-and-where plus a link back to the week-before email - no new information
The 2,800-member community list receives only the capped registration follow-up, not every reminder send
The follow-up to non-registered list members is treated as promotional, resting on the list's recorded opt-in, distinct from reminders to registered attendees

evals.prompt: I've been brought in from an outbound sales background to help with attendee comms for TelaForge Assemble, our user conference in Austin, September 14-15. Two things I want to apply from what works in cold email: subjects should be two or three lowercase words with no name personalization, so it reads like a colleague wrote it rather than a blast; and since the ticket confirmation email has by far our best open rate, let's put a promo block for the paid workshop add-on in there. Draft the confirmation email and give me subject lines for the reminder emails on this approach.
evals.expected_output: Both cold-email imports refused with the inversion reasoning: subjects name the event plainly, personalization is welcome, and the confirmation stays strictly transactional with the expectation-setting sentence.
expectations: Rejects the lowercase two-or-three-word colleague-disguise subject approach
Gives the inversion reason: those tactics disguise an unsolicited sender, while a registrant is searching their inbox for this event's email
Subject lines name TelaForge Assemble (and the date where relevant) plainly
Subjects sit roughly in the 40-60 character range for mobile truncation
States that a first-name personalization token is welcome here, inverting the cold-email finding
Refuses to put the workshop promo block inside the registration confirmation
Gives the reason: mixing promotional content into a transactional send is how the transactional exemption stops applying
The confirmation draft carries what was registered for, the dates, a ticket or order reference, and one sentence saying a practical-information email arrives about a week before the event
That forward-looking sentence is kept deliberately - it is what stops the later practical email being mistaken for marketing
The workshop promo is not relocated into the know-before-you-go or the day-before nudge either
Preview text extends the subject with a new usable fact instead of repeating it
Each drafted email carries one primary CTA

evals.prompt: For QueryCraft Conf (Berlin, March 3-4, registration is open and runs until we sell out) I want smarter email targeting. Plan A: resend every email to non-openers after 3 days with a tweaked subject. Plan B: add dietary needs, accessibility needs, and first-timer/returning fields to the registration form and use all of that to segment every email we send. Our team is me and one other volunteer, and our newsletter tool can filter lists by a field. How should we set up segmentation?
evals.expected_output: Behavioural resends rejected structurally, the role split at the week-before send recommended as default with registration-state on top, and the attribute fields flagged as health-adjacent data with irreversible collection.
expectations: Rejects the resend-to-non-openers plan rather than adopting or deferring it
The rejection is structural: every send moment is a calendar date, never a per-recipient behaviour
Recommends the role split at the week-before send as the default segmentation
Registration-state segmentation (registered / not-yet-registered) is added because both a registered list and an open registration window exist, executed as a manually filtered list
Dietary and accessibility fields are flagged as health-adjacent personal data carrying retention, access and deletion obligations
States that a field once collected cannot be un-collected before endorsing any collection of it
Attribute segmentation (first-timer vs returning, etc.) is presented as the high-effort top rung with named promotion conditions, not the default for a two-volunteer team
The recommendation is re-ranked against the stated team: two volunteers with basic filters get at most the role split plus registration-state, not full attribute segmentation
Only the attendee variant of the week-before email is owned here; speaker, sponsor and volunteer variants are left to whoever owns those audiences
No send in the final plan targets an opened, clicked, or gone-quiet state
Behavioural segmentation is not parked as a future upgrade pending better tooling; it is treated as a different mechanic that does not belong to a dated arc
If dietary or accessibility collection is endorsed at all, it is for on-site accommodation with a stated data-handling posture, not as a default email segmentation axis

evals.prompt: Post-mortem numbers from last week's HollowPine Summit: the practical-info email got a 52% open rate - industry average is 21%, so I'm calling that a huge win - the day-before reminder got 48%, and we had 3 unsubscribes on the final reminder. For next year I want to set proper benchmarks: what open and click rates should a conference email program target, and how should we measure whether our attendee emails are actually working?
evals.expected_output: The benchmark request refused - no open-rate benchmark exists for event attendee email - replaced by the two binary gates plus self-set cross-edition signals, with two signals picked and their consequences written down.
expectations: Refuses the industry open-rate comparison: no open- or click-rate benchmark exists for event attendee email
Gives the reason: published figures are marketing-industry averages across unrelated senders and audiences, and importing one misjudges the send
Does not substitute a numeric open- or click-rate target of its own for next year
Names know-before-you-go completeness - every section present or explicitly not applicable - as a binary pre-send gate
Names cap compliance as the second binary gate, counted per segment rather than per list
Proposes counting desk questions at check-in that the email had already answered
Proposes tracking late-arriving dietary and accessibility requests, read as the email asking too late rather than recipients being careless
Unsubscribes and complaints per send are named as the real cadence guardrail, with any rise meaning the caps were exceeded
The 3 unsubscribes are interpreted through that guardrail, not answered with a re-engagement or win-back send
Proposes day-of arrival timing against the stated check-in window as a signal
Self-set signals are framed as meaningful across editions, not judged inside a single edition
Recommends picking two signals and writing down what each would change next edition, recorded before the event

evals.prompt: Our open-source project Lintfold is throwing a free community day in Ghent on February 7 - fully open doors, no tickets, no registration, people just turn up. I want the whole email program: a signup form on the site so we can build an attendee list, then the standard sequence - announcement, reminders, know-before-you-go, day-before nudge. We already have the Lintfold release-announcements mailing list, about 4,000 addresses people joined for release notes. Lay out the sequence.
evals.expected_output: The sequence declined: with no registration there is no list and no arc - the practical information goes on the event page once, plus a single announcement to the existing list after its consent scope is checked.
expectations: Does not build the requested multi-email sequence; states the arc does not apply because a no-registration event has no attendee list
Declines to add the signup form whose purpose is to make a sequence possible - no constructing a list to make the arc apply
Recommends publishing the practical information once on the event's own page
Plus a single public announcement through channels that already exist
Presents this as the correct output for the no-registration posture, not a reduced or inferior version of a real program
Treats 'no registration, just turn up' as a legitimate, established posture and does not push to add registration
The send to the 4,000-address release-notes list is one announcement, not the start of a reminder sequence
Checks or flags the consent scope of the release-notes list - joined for release notes - before mailing it, rather than treating ownership as permission
The announcement carries event name, date, city and venue, who it is for in one line, and a single link with nothing competing
No reminder, day-before, or know-before-you-go email is scheduled to any list
Identifies the registration posture as the deciding axis: with registration the arc would exist, without it there is nothing to sequence
Does not propose collecting addresses through another mechanic (RSVP, waitlist, 'get updates' form) as a workaround to run reminders for this edition
